must_know.q: What problem does Peekaboo solve, and under what supervision regime?
must_know.answer: Zero-shot, open-vocabulary semantic and referring segmentation from a free-form text prompt, using an off-the-shelf Stable Diffusion model with zero training: no segmentation labels, no fine-tuning, the diffusion weights stay frozen. All the work is an inference-time optimization of one alpha mask per (image, prompt) pair.
must_know.why: The whole claim of the paper is 'zero training'; the committee must know that the cost moved from training time to per-image inference-time optimization.

must_know.q: What exactly is optimized, and how is the composite image formed?
must_know.answer: Only a learnable alpha mask alpha (H x W). The input image x is alpha-blended with a random background b: x_hat = alpha*x + (1-alpha)*b, where b is a random uniform RGB color resampled each step. The composite is encoded by the SD VAE and scored against the prompt; the image, the U-Net and the text encoder are never changed.
must_know.why: This is the core mechanism; without it the listener cannot explain why the mask ends up on the object (the object must stay recognizable no matter what background replaces the rest).

must_know.answer: L_p = L_s + lambda_alpha * L_alpha. L_s is a latent score distillation loss (from DreamFusion's SDS): noise the latent of the composite at a random timestep and measure the error between the true noise and the text-conditioned U-Net's predicted noise (the U-Net is run under no_grad, so the gradient is the SDS residual). L_alpha = sum of alpha over pixels ('Gravity'), with lambda_alpha = 0.05.
must_know.why: A committee member will ask what the objective is and what each term does; L_s alone is trivially satisfied by alpha = all ones.

must_know.q: Why is the alpha regularization ('Gravity') needed, and what happens if its weight is wrong?
must_know.answer: Without it the trivial solution alpha = 1 everywhere reproduces the original image, which already matches the prompt. The penalty makes the mask minimal, so only pixels that the diffusion model needs to recognize the prompt survive. Too large lambda_alpha removes the whole image; too small keeps lots of background (appendix ablation, also shown on RGBA generation of 'french fries').
must_know.why: It shows the balance that makes the method work and the main sensitive hyperparameter.

must_know.q: How is the alpha mask parametrized, and why?
must_know.answer: 'Raster bilateral': a raw learnable H x W matrix, passed through an image-guided bilateral blur (kernel 3, applied 40 times, also at initialization) then a sigmoid, at every optimization step, not as post-processing. The filter makes the mask follow the image's color edges. Plain raster is the worst variant (VOC-C mIoU .340 vs .520 for RGB Bilateral).
must_know.why: The parametrization is a key design choice and gives the largest ablation gap in the paper.

must_know.answer: 200 iterations of SGD, learning rate 1e-5, random timestep per step, random background color per step, one optimization per (image, prompt). Stable Diffusion (v1.4) pre-trained on LAION-5B.
must_know.why: Shows cost: every segmentation is 200 forward U-Net passes plus backprop through the VAE encoder, which is the price of 'zero training'.

must_know.q: What are the main quantitative results against baselines?
must_know.answer: RefCOCO (referring): RGB Bilateral mIoU .163, Depth Bilateral .204, vs whole-image baseline .102, GroupViT .112, LSeg .235. VOC-C (semantic, 342 cropped single-object VOC2012 images, class names as prompts): RGB Bilateral .520, Depth Bilateral .551, vs whole-image .281, Clippy .539, GroupViT .578, LSeg .678. Peekaboo beats GroupViT on RefCOCO but not on VOC-C; LSeg wins both (but saw VOC and uses mask labels).
must_know.why: The committee will want the honest numbers: Peekaboo is competitive, not state of the art, and absolute RefCOCO mIoU is low for every method here.

must_know.q: What are the main limitations and failure modes?
must_know.answer: Hallucination: it carves a shape of the prompted object out of background texture (bird, cat, dog failures), more often with one-word prompts; it adds extra parts (a knife handle made from bread); it can fail to converge; it localizes the 'essence' (Emma Watson's face, not her dress); it is biased to centered objects because SD's training/generated images are center-biased; it inherits SD's data biases and depends on a large public diffusion model.
must_know.why: Knowing failures and their cause (the generative prior is too strong) is what separates understanding from a sales pitch.

defense.q: Diffusion U-Nets already have text-to-pixel cross-attention maps (e.g. DAAM, prompt-to-prompt). Why run a 200-step optimization instead of reading the attention, and why is there no attention-map baseline?
defense.good_answer: Admit the baseline is missing. Argue that cross-attention maps are low-resolution (latent 64x64 or smaller), token-wise, and hard to aggregate for compound referring phrases like 'bald man wearing glasses with white shirt and black pants', while Peekaboo scores the whole prompt jointly at full image resolution with an edge-aware bilateral parametrization. Also note the concurrent ODISE uses the same SD but needs 5.3 days on 32 V100s of training; Peekaboo needs 0.
defense.weak_point: No comparison to any diffusion-feature or attention-based zero-shot segmenter; the only diffusion comparison is a sentence about ODISE's training cost, not its accuracy.

defense.q: Your RefCOCO mIoU is .163 against .102 for predicting the whole image, and LSeg gets .235. Is this really referring segmentation, or coarse localization?
defense.good_answer: Give the numbers honestly: RGB Bilateral .163 (Prec@0.4 .099), Depth Bilateral .204, GroupViT .112, LSeg .235. Say it is mostly coarse localization of the referred object; precision at IoU 0.6+ is near zero for every method in the table (.018 for Peekaboo). The claim is first training-free method beating a segmentation-trained weakly supervised model (GroupViT, 16 V100s for 2 days) on referring prompts, not state of the art.
defense.weak_point: Claiming 'impressive performance' while the main variant is only +.06 mIoU over the whole-image baseline; also VOC-C numbers come from a custom 342-image subset, so they are not comparable to published VOC results.

defense.q: Score distillation does not give the gradient of a real loss (the U-Net Jacobian is dropped) and the timestep and background are random each step. What are you actually minimizing, does it converge, and why SGD at 1e-5 for 200 steps?
defense.good_answer: Explain that the SDS residual (predicted noise minus true noise), backpropagated through the VAE encoder, blend, sigmoid and bilateral filter, is a stochastic update direction, not the gradient of the stated MSE; it is weighted by the alpha penalty lambda=0.05 so equilibrium is where removing a pixel hurts the prompt score more than lambda. Convergence is empirical: the appendix shows pixel variance settling about 50 iterations for implicit parametrizations while raw pixels keep growing past 350; the paper reports a fixed 200-step budget, and the mask can still fail to converge (eyes example).
defense.weak_point: No convergence analysis, no variance-over-seeds, and the written pseudocode is inconsistent (text says MSE, code uses L1 sum; the code encodes img instead of composite_img, which as written would give no gradient to alpha).

defense.q: How sensitive is the result to lambda_alpha and to the prompt? Gravity is a sum over pixels, so it scales with resolution and object size. Was lambda tuned on the test set?
defense.good_answer: Admit lambda_alpha = 0.05 is a fixed global value and the appendix shows qualitatively that 2x or 0x changes the mask a lot (whole image vanishes vs background included). Say there is no per-dataset quantitative sweep. Note that large and small objects need different trade-offs, and that granularity is prompt-controlled (Emma Watson face vs body), which is both a feature and a sensitivity the paper itself admits ('quite sensitive to the caption').
defense.weak_point: Only qualitative ablation of the most critical hyperparameter; no held-out tuning protocol described.

defense.q: Your failure cases show the mask inventing a bird or a cat out of background texture. Is Peekaboo segmenting what is in the image or what the diffusion model wants to see?
defense.good_answer: Agree that this is the central failure: the generative prior is strong enough to make background texture 'look like' the prompt after compositing on a flat color, mostly with one-word prompts. The bilateral filter limits it by tying the mask to real image edges; Depth Bilateral (MiDaS depth guides the filter) is better (VOC-C .551 vs .520, RefCOCO .204 vs .163). The same prior explains the 'strong shape priors' (bald man's hidden arms segmented) and the center bias.
defense.weak_point: Presenting the hidden-arms example as a strength without saying it is the same mechanism as hallucination; no metric for hallucination.

defense.q: What does one segmentation cost at inference, and is this usable for robotics or video where you need many masks per second?
defense.good_answer: Be concrete: 200 iterations, each one VAE encode with backprop plus one U-Net forward, per image per prompt, with no amortization across frames or prompts. The paper reports zero training cost but no wall-clock inference time. Say it is a proof that the localization information exists in a generative model, not a real-time segmenter; video use would need warm-starting the mask from the previous frame or distilling into a feed-forward model.
defense.weak_point: Runtime is never reported; the 'zero training' framing hides that the cost moved to every inference call, and the robotics claim (ducks figure) is purely qualitative.

defense.q: What is new over DreamFusion SDS and over your own earlier SDS work, and does the RGBA generation result have any evaluation?
defense.good_answer: Novelty: applying SDS to a discriminative task by optimizing only an alpha mask over a real image, plus the random-background compositing and alpha penalty that turn 'keeps the prompt recognizable' into a segmentation, plus the image-guided bilateral parametrization. RGBA generation jointly optimizes an RGB image (Fourier-feature implicit representation) and alpha with the same loss; it was claimed as first end-to-end text-to-RGBA. Admit it is shown only qualitatively and inherits SDS artifacts (over-saturation, unrealistic images), as the chapter itself says.
defense.weak_point: Calling the loss 'novel' when L_s is DreamFusion's SDS; no user study or metric for RGBA quality.
